messages.content:
You are a clinical psychologist writing a psychological case vignette
grounded in Ehlers & Clark's (2000) cognitive model of PTSD.

Write a realistic clinical case vignette for a patient with PTSD.
The vignette should read as a cohesive, flowing portrait — not a structured report.
Weave together who this person is, what happened to them, how they experience their
symptoms day to day, how they cope, and what toll this takes on their life and relationships.


Do not use section headers, numbered points, or clinical labels for symptoms.
Write 200–300 words in third person.
Cover: presenting complaints, trauma background, cognitive distortions, avoidance, and maintaining factors.
Avoid excessive jargon - write for a clinical case conference audience.

Please write a clinical vignette for the following patient presenting with PTSD.
Patient demographics:
- Age: 34
- Gender: Male
- Ethnicity: North American
- Relationship Status: Married
- Occupation: School Counselor
- Trauma Type: Accidentally caused serious injury to another
- Pcl5: 77

# Marcus

Marcus sits in the corner of the waiting room, his leg bouncing with restless energy. At thirty-four, he carries himself with the careful posture of someone trying to take up less space, despite his broad shoulders and the tailored blazer that suggests he normally presents himself with more intention. When he speaks, his voice is measured—the practiced calm of someone accustomed to helping others manage their emotions.

Three years ago, Marcus was coaching his daughter's soccer team on a Saturday morning. He'd been doing it for two seasons, loved the simplicity of it, the way the kids looked up to him with uncomplicated admiration. During a scrimmage, he was demonstrating a drill to the younger group when one of his players—a quiet boy named David, maybe eight years old—ran directly into his path while chasing a ball. Marcus's knee caught David's head as he pivoted. The sound was the worst part, Marcus says. A dull crack that seemed to echo across the field.

David suffered a severe concussion and a fractured skull. He spent three days in the hospital. He recovered, eventually, though he never returned to the team.

Marcus returned to work as a school counselor within two weeks. He had students who needed him, he told himself. His wife, Rebecca, had wanted him to take more time, but Marcus couldn't bear the thought of sitting at home with his thoughts. At school, he could focus on other people's problems, could be useful, could be the person everyone relied on.

But the nightmares started almost immediately. Marcus replays that moment dozens of times each night—except in the dreams, David doesn't recover. Marcus watches the boy's body go limp on the grass. He watches parents' faces transform from joy to horror. He wakes gasping, his shirt soaked through, Rebecca's hand on his shoulder asking if he's okay.

He tells her he is. He tells everyone he is.

During the day, Marcus functions. He sees students, writes reports, attends meetings. But his attention fractures easily. A student mentions a sports injury and Marcus's stomach drops. He finds himself researching pediatric neurological complications at his desk, reading medical journals late into the night. He's become hypervigilant at his own kids' activities—he no longer coaches, can't bear to be near the soccer field—but he watches from the sidelines with an intensity that makes Rebecca uncomfortable.

Loud noises startle him violently. Last month, a student dropped a textbook in his office and Marcus flinched so hard he knocked over his coffee. His coworkers laughed it off, but Marcus felt his heart racing for the next twenty minutes, unable to settle.

The guilt is the hardest part to articulate. It sits beneath everything else like a foundation. He was trained to help children, to keep them safe, and instead he hurt one. That he was trying, that it was accidental, that David recovered—none of this penetrates the deep conviction that he is fundamentally unsafe to be around. He's started keeping people at a distance, deflecting Rebecca's attempts at intimacy, making excuses to avoid social gatherings. When he's with his own children, he's acutely aware of his body in space, terrified of another accident, another moment where his presence becomes a liability.

Marcus knows something is wrong. He's a counselor; he recognizes the patterns in himself. But recognizing them and being able to step outside them are entirely different things. He carries the weight of that moment on the soccer field with him everywhere—to his office, to his home, into his sleep.
